# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Element, particularly those valuing data ownership and self-hosting capabilities. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free for self-hosted instances, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Slack's data ownership policy is more restrictive.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosted instances, compared to Slack's straightforward onboarding process.
* Scalability: Slack is generally more scalable, with more advanced features for large teams, while Element's scalability depends on the self-hosted infrastructure.
* Integration with external services: Slack has more extensive integration with third-party services, such as Google Drive and Trello, while Element focuses on more secure, decentralized integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Extensive integration with third-party services
* Scalable for large teams
* User-friendly interface
* Limited data ownership and control
### Element
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Free for self-hosted instances
* Secure, decentralized architecture
* Customizable and extensible
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup

## When to Choose Each
Slack is suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use, scalability, and integration with external services. It's ideal for large teams or those who don't require full data ownership. On the other hand, Element is perfect for teams that value data ownership, security, and customization. It's suitable for teams of all sizes, especially those with technical expertise, who want full control over their communication platform.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data in JSON format using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server, either self-hosted or using a managed service.
3. Use the Element import tool to migrate your data from the JSON export.
4. Configure your Element instance, including setting up users, channels, and integrations.
5. Test your Element instance to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its complexity and limited user support. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is Element's limited support for certain file types and integrations. However, for teams that value data ownership and security, Element is a viable alternative to Slack, and we recommend considering it for teams with technical expertise.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need extensive integration with external services
* Technical teams who value data ownership and security
* Organizations with strict data control requirements
* Teams with existing self-hosted infrastructure
* Developers who want a customizable communication platform

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Element?
Yes, Element can be self-hosted, giving teams full control over their data and infrastructure.
### Is Element free?
Element is free for self-hosted instances, but managed services may charge a fee.
### Can I integrate Element with Google Drive?
Element has limited integration with Google Drive, but it's possible using third-party services or custom integrations.
### Is Slack more scalable than Element?
Yes, Slack is generally more scalable, with more advanced features for large teams.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can migrate your Slack data to Element using the Element import tool and a JSON export from Slack.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for teams, offering features such as messaging, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison benefits teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and cost-effectiveness. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and a key reason to switch is to gain more control over data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their data on their own servers, while Slack stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup Complexity: Mattermost requires more technical expertise to set up and manage, while Slack offers a simpler, cloud-based solution.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed for large, distributed teams and can scale to meet the needs of enterprises, while Slack also offers scalable solutions but at a higher cost.
* Integration: Mattermost offers a more extensive range of customization options and integrations with other tools, including the ability to integrate with GitHub and Jira, while Slack has a more limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with other tools
* Simple, intuitive interface
* Scalable solutions for large teams
* Limited customization options
### Mattermost
* Free, self-hosted option
* High degree of customization and integration
* Designed for large, distributed teams
* More control over data and security
* Steeper learning curve and more technical expertise required

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations. It is also a good option for teams that do not require a high degree of customization or control over their data. Mattermost, on the other hand, is a better choice for large, distributed teams that require a high degree of customization and control over their data. It is also a good option for teams that prioritize data ownership and security.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack Export tool, which produces a JSON file.
2. Set up a Mattermost server and configure the necessary integrations and customizations.
3. Use the Mattermost Import tool to import your Slack data from the JSON file.
4. Test and verify that all data and integrations are working correctly.
5. Train your team on the use of Mattermost and its features.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a high degree of customization and control over data. However, it does require more technical expertise to set up and manage, which can be a limitation for some teams. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's mobile app can be less polished than Slack's, which may be a consideration for teams with a high number of mobile users. Overall, we recommend switching to Mattermost for teams that prioritize data ownership and control, and are willing to invest the time and expertise required to set up and manage the platform.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not require a high degree of customization and are looking for a free, self-hosted solution.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that prioritize data ownership and control, and are willing to invest the time and expertise required to set up and manage Mattermost.
* Large, distributed teams (more than 50 users) that require a high degree of customization and control over their data.
* Teams that do not require a wide range of integrations with other tools.
* Teams that prioritize security and data ownership, and are willing to invest in the necessary infrastructure and expertise.

## FAQ
### Can I use Mattermost for free?
Yes, Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option that can be used by teams of any size.
### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
No, Mattermost requires more technical expertise to set up and manage, and has a steeper learning curve.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with other tools?
Yes, Mattermost offers a high degree of customization and integration with other tools, including GitHub and Jira.
### Is Mattermost secure?
Yes, Mattermost is designed with security in mind, and offers a high degree of control over data and access.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers an import tool that allows you to migrate your Slack data from a JSON file.

# Discord vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Discord and Element are communication platforms designed for communities and teams, offering features such as messaging, voice and video calls, and file sharing. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution, with a key reason being data ownership and control. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration and community building.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is free and self-hosted, with costs limited to server maintenance.
* Data Ownership: Element allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Discord's terms of service grant the company rights to use and distribute user content.
* Setup Complexity: Discord has a more straightforward setup process, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element is highly scalable due to its self-hosted nature, allowing users to add more servers as needed, whereas Discord's scalability is limited by its proprietary infrastructure.
* Feature Difference: Element offers end-to-end encryption by default, while Discord only offers encryption for direct messages.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $4.99/month (Nitro subscription) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4.99/month (Nitro subscription) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Discord
* Pros:
	+ Easy to use and set up
	+ Large user base and community
	+ Robust features for gaming and streaming
	+ Mobile apps available
* Cons:
	+ Limited control over data
	+ Proprietary license
	+ Limited scalability
	+ End-to-end encryption not enabled by default
### Element
* Pros:
	+ Self-hosted and open-source
	+ End-to-end encryption by default
	+ Highly scalable
	+ Retain full ownership of data
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited mobile app functionality
	+ Requires technical expertise for self-hosting
	+ Limited support for gaming and streaming

## When to Choose Each
Discord is suitable for small to medium-sized teams, especially those in the gaming and streaming communities, who prioritize ease of use and a large user base. On the other hand, Element is ideal for larger organizations or communities that require high scalability, data ownership, and control, such as enterprises or government institutions.

Element is a better fit for teams that value security and transparency, with its end-to-end encryption and open-source nature. Additionally, teams with the technical expertise to self-host a server can benefit from Element's customizability and cost-effectiveness.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Discord server data using the Discord API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Import your exported data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure any additional features or integrations as needed.
5. Test your Element server to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its technical requirements and limited mobile app functionality. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's self-hosted nature requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain. However, for teams that value data ownership and security, Element is a clear choice, and we recommend switching from Discord to Element if you have the technical expertise and prioritize these features.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of 10-20 users who prioritize data ownership and security
* Medium-sized teams of 50-100 users who require high scalability
* Large enterprises with 200+ users who need customizability and cost-effectiveness
* Communities that do not require gaming or streaming features

No, Element is not optimized for gaming and streaming, and its features are limited in this regard.
### Is Element free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, with costs limited to server maintenance.
### Can I self-host Discord?
No, Discord does not offer self-hosting options.
### Is Element end-to-end encrypted?
Yes, Element offers end-to-end encryption by default.
### Can I import my Discord data into Element?
Yes, you can export your Discord data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

* Scalability: AppFlowy is designed to be highly scalable, making it a good choice for large teams, while Notion can become expensive for large teams.

AppFlowy, on the other hand, is a good choice for large teams or organizations who need a highly scalable and customizable collaboration tool. However, for teams who require self-hosting and want full control over their data, AppFlowy is a good choice. title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control systems used for software development. This comparison is beneficial for developers, teams, and organizations looking to choose between the two platforms for their core use case of collaborative coding and project management. The key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data, reduce costs, or utilize specific features.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free public repositories, while GitLab offers free self-hosted repositories.
* Data ownership: GitLab allows users to self-host their repositories, giving them full control over their data, whereas GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: GitLab is more complex to set up, especially for self-hosted repositories, while GitHub is generally easier to use.
* Scalability: Both platforms are highly scalable, but GitLab's self-hosted option allows for more flexibility.
* Feature difference: GitLab offers a built-in Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) tool, while GitHub relies on third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and ecosystem
* Robust security features
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Limited control over data
**GitLab:**
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* Built-in CI/CD tool
* Highly customizable
* Free for self-hosted repositories
* Can be complex to set up and manage

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data. It's also ideal for teams that are already invested in the GitHub ecosystem. On the other hand, GitLab is a better choice for larger teams or organizations that require more control over their data, customization options, and advanced features like built-in CI/CD.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Archive format.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and navigate to the import page.
3. Use the GitLab import tool to import your GitHub repository.
4. Update any existing links or references to point to the new GitLab repository.
5. Test and verify that all data and functionality have been migrated successfully.

## Our Take
GitLab is production-ready for most users, offering a robust and feature-rich platform. However, one technical limitation to consider is the potential complexity of setting up and managing self-hosted repositories. For teams that require a high degree of customization and control over their data, GitLab is an excellent choice, but for smaller teams or those prioritizing ease of use, GitHub may still be the better option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that require self-hosted repositories and don't need GitHub's ecosystem
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that need built-in CI/CD and don't require GitHub's proprietary features
* Large teams (over 50 users) that prioritize data control and customization options
* Teams that require advanced security features and don't need GitHub's ease of use
* Organizations with existing self-hosted infrastructure that can support GitLab

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
GitLab offers a free self-hosted option, as well as a free tier for its cloud-based service. However, the free tier has some limitations, and larger teams may need to upgrade to a paid plan.
### Can I use GitLab for personal projects?
Yes, GitLab is suitable for personal projects, and its free self-hosted option makes it an attractive choice for individuals who want full control over their data.
### Is GitHub better for small teams?
GitHub is generally easier to use and set up, making it a good choice for small teams that prioritize ease of use. However, GitLab's free self-hosted option can be a cost-effective solution for small teams that require more control over their data.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to GitLab?
Yes, you can migrate your GitHub repository to GitLab using the GitLab import tool. The process is relatively straightforward, but may require some technical expertise.
### Does GitLab offer customer support?
GitLab offers various support options, including community support, documentation, and paid support plans for enterprise customers.

title: GitHub vs Gitea
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are two popular design and collaboration tools used by teams to create, test, and refine user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) designs. This comparison is beneficial for designers, product managers, and developers who are looking for a cost-effective and self-hosted solution, with the key reason to switch being the need for data ownership and control. The core use case for both tools is collaborative design, with Penpot offering a free and open-source alternative.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data, while Figma stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup Complexity: Figma has a more user-friendly interface and is easier to set up, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Figma is designed to handle large teams and complex projects, while Penpot is still developing its scalability features.
* Feature Difference: Figma has a more comprehensive set of design tools and integrations, including a built-in prototype tool, while Penpot relies on third-party integrations for some features.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface
	+ Comprehensive set of design tools
	+ Large community and support resources
	+ Scalable and reliable infrastructure
	+ Integrates with many third-party tools
* Cons:
	+ Expensive for large teams
	+ Limited control over data storage and security
	+ Proprietary license
### Penpot
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option for data control and security
	+ Customizable and extensible
	+ Growing community and support resources
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited scalability features
	+ Fewer integrations with third-party tools
	+ Still in active development

## When to Choose Each
Figma is the better choice for large teams and complex projects that require a comprehensive set of design tools and integrations, as well as a scalable and reliable infrastructure. It is also a good option for teams that prioritize ease of use and are willing to pay for the convenience.
Penpot, on the other hand, is the better choice for teams that prioritize data ownership and control, as well as cost-effectiveness. It is also a good option for teams that are comfortable with self-hosting and customizing their design tools, and are looking for a free and open-source solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in the Figma API JSON format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to convert your Figma designs into Penpot files.
3. Review and update your designs to take advantage of Penpot's features and customization options.
4. Set up your Penpot self-hosted server and configure it to your needs.
5. Invite your team to join your Penpot instance and start collaborating on your designs.

## Our Take
Penpot is still in active development, and while it shows promise, it may not be production-ready for most users right now. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's scalability features are still limited, and large teams may experience performance issues.
However, for teams that prioritize data ownership and control, as well as cost-effectiveness, Penpot is definitely worth considering. We recommend switching to Penpot if you are a small to medium-sized team with simple design needs and are comfortable with self-hosting and customizing your design tools.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that prioritize cost-effectiveness and data ownership
* Teams that do not need advanced design tools and integrations
* Teams that are comfortable with self-hosting and customizing their design tools
* Teams that prioritize open-source and community-driven development
* Solo designers or freelancers who want a free and customizable design solution

## FAQ
### Is Penpot completely free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free and open-source, with no costs or licensing fees.
### Can I self-host Penpot?
Yes, Penpot offers a self-hosting option, which allows you to have full control over your data and security.
### Is Penpot compatible with Figma files?
Yes, Penpot has an import tool that allows you to convert Figma designs into Penpot files.
### Does Penpot have a user-friendly interface?
No, Penpot has a steeper learning curve than Figma, and its interface is not as user-friendly.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams?
Not yet, Penpot's scalability features are still limited, and large teams may experience performance issues.
